review: FC1 the enemy will engage you beyond the render distance if you're in the open. This is what happens when enemies are actually aware of how much of a threat the main character poses.

Far Cry deserves its place in the pantheon of "Legendary FPS games". Released in 2004, even today it is comfortably better than many so-called "AAA" games released in the modern age. At the time of coming to market, Far Cry set new benchmarks for AI, graphics and gameplay. Loading was a thing of the past, with massive maps, near-unlimited draw distance, and missions which had multiple approaches to completing.

Unfortunately, the version on Steam has the broken AI, which basically gives the enemies X-Ray vision (you can search online for enemies tracking and shooting players through cover). I played with FCAM (Far Cry Addon Mod), which fixes the AI, enhances the graphics, adds ironsights to the weapons, introduces quicksave functionality, amongst other things). There are other ways to get around the AI issue, but they are far more tedious and less likely to work. Strongly recommend getting FCAM and playing with it enabled. Should you decide to go this route, append "-mod:FCAM" to the launch options, minus the quotation marks: this will launch the game and FCAM mod automatically, saving you from having to manually switch from the main menu.

For those complaining about the difficulty, this is not a run-and-gun shooter: the enemies are smart, and will home in on your location, and attempt to surround or flank you. Staying on the move constantly is key to success, as well as choosing your battleground carefully. Pro tip: pre-aim for the head, you'll drop enemies much faster.

Played on Windows 10 Pro x64 with only two or three crashes - each time, a restart of the game was sufficient.

HIghly recommended to anyone who enjoys FPS games - this one cannot be missed and is a true classic (the daddy of Crysis).

EDIT: The FCAM version you want is v1.999 - this was the final release.

This is a fairly good game. In 2004, when it came out, it was met with great opposition. I'm not referring to the critics either. 2004 was probably the biggest milestone in first person shooters since 1992ish. The same year this classic Far Cry title came out, the world was also met with Half-Life 2 and Doom 3. All 3 of these titles managed to stun and impress the gaming community with not only some of the greatest visuals seen at the time but some of the most innovative gaming engines and gameplay features we had seen in many years.

Where Half-Life 2 had the phenomenal Source engine and its spectacular physics and Doom 3 had the unbeatable dynamic lights and shadows, Far Cry had the best feature of them all: a (semi) non-linear game map style with proper jungle based stealth.

Unlike the typical first person shooter of the time (and still ever present today) this Crytek title brought the player choices. Not choices in how the game evolved or ended story-wise, but choices in gameplay STYLE. You didn't have to run and gun the entire game if you didn't want to. For once, the player could crouch or go prone in tall grass and sneak up or around enemies without being detected. The player could get in close with a machete and perform stealth kills. The player could also throw rocks to distract the enemies so further the effect.

To add to this amazing stealth based (optional) approach to the gameplay, the player could also choose roughly which path they wanted to take as the levels progressed. The levels always have a point A and a point B. The player could however, choose how they reached point B. You can fly half the way in a hang glider. You could speed your way there in a truck. You could work your way around the edges of the map in a boat. You could sneak through the jungle. You could flat out mow everyone down with machine guns and waltz the heck right in. The point is this; you weren't forced to do as the game wanted you to do as though stuck on rails.

The gameplay made this one of the top titles for years. This was also one of the first if not THE first title to experiment with a 64-bit executable. I don't recall if this Steam version has that executable but I DO recall not being able to get it working properly and without texture glitches on an Intel CPU. Regardless, this was a monumental release, even if the story was lame and the gameplay has since grown tired for me. Frankly, I much prefer the Ubisoft Far Cry titles nowadays as they have evolved very well without losing the character of the original.

This is a game all FPS fans should try so they can experience FPS history at one of its finest moments.

Reading the negative reviews for this has upset me a little.  It seems that the two main complaints people have are that the game is too hard and the story is somewhat lame.  

I would agree that this is a hard game, it does not baby the player.  There is no regenerating health, the enemy soldiers move quickly and have decent aim.  I am not great at FPS games, but playing this game on medium is very enjoyable to me.  The checkpoints are very well spaced.  There are just enough health and armor packs. 

 If you are getting stuck in one spot I would suggest trying a different approach.  Maybe even back up one checkpoint and come it things from a different angle.  This is very different from the modern corridor shooters.  The maps are enormous and you are free to go anywhere.  I can see how this could be confusing for younger gamers used to COD style gameplay.  Boats and trucks are an excellent strategy with their mounted guns.  Stealth works very also.  Early game with the M16 switching to single shot mode, going prone and headshots from a distance is another good method.  Rushing in and spraying bullets will not work as well.  

You will have ample ammo for your pistol and assault rifle, but much less for speciailzed weapons like the sniper rifle and rpg.  This keeps things balanced and rewards the player for good planning.  

Final comments on the difficulty.  Everyone has different levels of skill.  For me on he hardest difficulty levels I can not get very far without getting stuck.  On medium the game is fun and I die maybe a couple times per level.  Select the level appropriate for your abilities.  Once you learn where the enemies are and how many that will give you an advantage.

Technologically this game is a masterpiece.  Released 10 years and still looks great.  It is the predecessor to Crysis.  As for the story, who cares?  It is a game not a movie.  It is about the gameplay here.  Cut scenes are few and far between and non disruptive.  Nothing gets between you and pulling that trigger.  There are no QTE's or moments where the game takes control away from you.  It is a very pure experience.

‘Farcry’ was originally a 2004 FPS game made from ‘Cryengine’ software from a German company called ‘Crytek’ who then moved onto the ‘Crysis’ franchise. Seriously ‘Crytek’ what is it with you and your obsession with the word cry? You ‘Cry babies’…

There was actually a ‘far cry’ at the time of this games release for an FPS that broke conventional form of being closed in, linear and dark. No engines at that time could handle both open worlds and at the same time be rich in colour, with large viewing distance and high definition. CryEngine was first demonstrated back at a 1999 expo with a demo called X-Isle Dinosaur Island https://youtu.be/wUqK5sgzTE0 this was really pushing the envelope at the time. Crytek then soon after struck a deal with NVidia to roll out X-isle with all Nvidia Cards. With CryEngine now being the most demanding game engine on the market, it soon led Ubisoft into agreeing to make X-Isle into a full AAA title game. After a bit of tweaking with idea’s (from dinosaur and aliens to mercenaries) this X-Isle then eventually transitioned into the Farcry Classic known today and released 2004.

After Farcry’s release, Crytek in the same year, signed a deal with EA to start producing the Crysis series with an even more improved CryEngine that they were working on. Due to EA being a direct competitor to Ubisoft, the Farcry series from then on, was largely assigned over to Ubisoft Montreal and were commissioned to port ‘Farcry’ over for consoles. Unfortunately consoles though at this point in time were simply not powerful enough to handle the wide-open levels. So, the whole game was practically rewritten to suit. This included Farcry Instincts 2005 (a reworked version of Farcry Classic with an alternate universe story), it’s sequel Farcry Evolution 2006 (a short continuation from the reworked version) Farcry Predator 2006 (A HD version of the previous two for Xbox 360) Farcry Vengeance 2007 for Wii (A reworked edition of Evolution with 3 levels added and which have no characters in it that actually died in Farcry Classic, meaning that it is most likely a cannon continuation for that one) and Paradise Lost 2007 a terrible money grabbing arcade version of Farcry Instincts. There was also a Farcry German novel Gotterdammerung 2007 which apparently puts you in the mind of a Trigen and Farcry the movie 2008 ( a low budget B-grade movie directed by Uwe Boll which does away with Doyle and Trigen and replaced them with an uncle and genetically engineered soldiers that have skin tougher than Kevlar vests, meaning they can only be shot in the eyes and mouth).

The reason I mention the above, is that the events pictured within, all above have to have taken place in the year 2025, regardless of being alternate universes or not.  This time line of events was cemented on the original license disk of Farcry. This means that the events pictured within, actually take place AFTER the nuclear holocaust, and AFTER the events depicted in Farcry 2 making that more a prequel. Still the problem is, with now three completely different versions of the original (movie included), which are as different as chalk and cheese. Which of the three should be considered original cannon and which one of the three stories should be considered as alternate universe? The answer to that question might lie with the 2014 release of 'Farcry Wild Expedition' which was an anniversary compendium which included 'Farcry Classic' in HD and NOT 'Farcry Instincts'. This means that the original cannon would be 'Farcry Classic' followed by 'Farcry Vengeance', and as stated before 'Farcry 2' a prequel and 'Farcry Instincts', 'Evolved' and 'Predator' all being alternate universe.

3.) There aren't that many vehicles but it's forgivable if you can drive something that fires rockets and wrecks entire campsites. 

4.) The A.I. enemies are impressive to fight against. Some operate like a squad and they tend to "think" (or pick stealth) more before assaulting your position.

6.) Graphics are nice, considering this game is over 10 years old.

 Link: http://forums.steampowered.com/forums/showthread.php?t=2092407

2.) Despite what some people said, a good portion of the campaign is linear, most notably the "indoor" parts. Also, the game doesn't do a good job in providing players with a diverse amount of alternative pathways to take. It usually only gives 2 avaliable walkways to complete the same objective and I do not find that acceptable. 


3.) There's some sort of A.I. bug in which the mercenaries can shoot at you accurately behind walls when you're in their bunkers.

4.) While I do not mind, a good amount of the Far Cry community despises the introduction of the "Trigens". In a way, I do agree with them because after you encounter them, the game becomes too different. 

5.) I was going to complain about the bland plot but the voice acting is far worse. The main character, Jack Carver, has a pretty bad voice actor and his lines are cliche'd. 

6.) Some sections of the game are notoriously hard, though not impossible to beat, even on easy. It would be understandable if you die almost immediately by rushing recklessly on the hardest difficulty but on easy is just overkill. The last level was hard but the worst part for me was fighting Crowe, the leader of the mercs, on a sinking boat while facing a helicopter. You only have a couple of minutes of destroy the aerial vehicle (as you cannot use a firearm when swimming), there's no supplies, and Crowe has good accuracy and he inflicts massive damage with his M249. 

7.) The worst thing Far Cry has is the "auto-save" and it lacks the ability for players to save manually whenever they want to. I heard that there is a console command as compensation but for those who don't know, they will have endless times of reloading an earlier save and you may even get stuck in a loop where you continuously perish. 

Summary: 

In all, I did enjoy the game after adjusting myself and giving it a 2nd try. However, $9.99 is too much as multiplayer and customization is dead so please get the game when it's at a discount if you're still interested. On the bright side, Far Cry does have more balls than its successors when it comes to difficulty.

[h1][b]Overview[/b][/h1]
Far Cry is a first-person shooter that blends open-ended combat with linear story progression across a chain of tropical islands. Players take the role of Jack Carver, a former Special Forces operative who becomes trapped in a conflict involving mercenaries, secret research, and increasingly dangerous enemies. Rather than relying solely on scripted corridors, the game encourages players to approach many encounters from different angles using stealth, long-range engagements, or direct assaults. Even decades after release, its large outdoor environments and freedom of approach remain defining features. It is best suited for players who enjoy challenging shooters and do not mind adapting to older game design conventions.

[h1][b]Gameplay[/b][/h1]
Far Cry revolves around exploring expansive maps, gathering weapons, and overcoming heavily guarded enemy positions. The open-level design allows players to scout patrol routes, use vegetation for cover, hijack vehicles, or attack head-on. This flexibility creates memorable encounters where improvisation is often rewarded.

Gunplay remains satisfying thanks to distinct weapon handling and responsive controls. Enemy AI is one of the game's strongest elements, as soldiers communicate, aggressively flank, and react to player positions more intelligently than in many shooters of its era. Unfortunately, the later portions introduce tougher mutated enemies that shift the focus toward durability rather than tactical combat, resulting in a noticeable drop in gameplay quality.

Difficulty can be demanding, especially on higher settings where enemies detect movement quickly and punish careless positioning. Checkpoint placement occasionally forces repeated sections after mistakes. Progression is straightforward without RPG mechanics, keeping the experience focused on combat and exploration. While pacing is excellent during the opening chapters, the second half loses some of its consistency due to repetitive encounters and changing enemy types.

[h1][b]Story & World[/b][/h1]
The narrative primarily exists to support the action rather than become its main attraction. Jack Carver is a capable but relatively simple protagonist, while most supporting characters fulfill familiar action movie roles. Dialogue is serviceable, though some performances feel dated.

The tropical islands remain the true highlight. Dense jungles, beaches, military compounds, caves, and research facilities create varied locations that naturally support different combat scenarios. The mystery surrounding the island keeps players engaged, although the writing never reaches the depth of stronger narrative-driven shooters. The story remains entertaining without overstaying its welcome.

[h1][b]Visual Presentation[/b][/h1]
CryEngine was groundbreaking at launch, and its influence is still easy to appreciate. Vast draw distances, dense vegetation, dynamic water, and convincing outdoor lighting helped establish a new benchmark for open environments.

Naturally, character models, facial animation, and textures now show their age. Despite this, the strong environmental art direction allows the islands to remain visually appealing. The interface is functional and unobtrusive, though clearly designed around early 2000s standards.

[h1][b]Audio[/b][/h1]
The soundtrack is used sparingly, allowing ambient jungle sounds to create most of the atmosphere. Wildlife, distant gunfire, explosions, and environmental effects greatly enhance immersion.

Weapon audio delivers satisfying impact, while voice acting ranges from competent to occasionally overacted. Audio quality is generally solid, although compression and recording quality reflect the technology available at the time.

[h1][b]Performance & Technical Quality[/b][/h1]
Modern hardware runs Far Cry with ease, offering high frame rates and short loading times. However, the original release has numerous compatibility issues on modern systems, including crashes, physics problems, widescreen limitations, and various graphical bugs depending on hardware and operating system.

Several important community fixes are required if the game is to be played without the original issues, and they are must-have installations rather than optional enhancements. Once properly configured, stability improves significantly, and the experience becomes much closer to what the developers originally intended. Graphics options remain respectable for a game of its age.

[h1][b]Content & Replayability[/b][/h1]
The campaign typically lasts around 15-20 hours depending on difficulty and playstyle. There is little traditional side content, but the sandbox nature of combat encourages experimenting with different tactics during repeat playthroughs.

The original release also includes multiplayer support, although finding active public matches today is limited. There is no New Game+, and achievement hunting depends on the platform version. Replayability comes primarily from mastering encounters rather than unlocking additional content.

[h1][b]Value for Money[/b][/h1]
Far Cry is frequently available at a very low price during Steam sales, making it an excellent value for players interested in classic first-person shooters. There are no microtransactions, and the complete experience is contained within the base game. While its age and required community fixes create a higher barrier to entry than modern alternatives, the amount of quality gameplay still justifies the asking price.

[h1][b]Pros[/b][/h1]
• Large and open combat arenas encourage multiple playstyles.
• Excellent enemy AI that remains impressive for its age.
• Strong environmental art direction with memorable tropical locations.
• Satisfying weapon variety and combat mechanics.
• Challenging gameplay rewards planning and positioning.
• Outstanding value during frequent Steam sales.

[h1][b]Cons[/b][/h1]
• The second half loses focus due to mutated enemy encounters.
• Original PC version requires several essential community fixes.
• Story and characters are functional but rarely memorable.
• Some checkpoint placement can become frustrating.
• Character models and animations have aged noticeably.
• Multiplayer community is now very limited.

[h1][b]Final Verdict[/b][/h1]
Far Cry remains an important milestone in the evolution of first-person shooters. Its combination of open-ended level design, intelligent enemy AI, and memorable tropical environments still provides an engaging experience despite its age. The campaign is held back by weaker late-game design decisions and technical problems that require community fixes, but once properly configured, it continues to demonstrate why it became such an influential title. Players willing to accept older design conventions will find a classic that still offers rewarding tactical combat and surprising freedom.

[b]Final Score: 83/100[/b]

For anyone playing for the first time, a recommendation with a warning. This is a classic, it feels like the logical evolution following games like Half-Life with a shooter that blends sci-fi but trying to ground it with some sense of realism and having a narrative through the levels instead of just maps, that said, unlike Half-Life and other shooters, this game can be really hard and the last couple of levers are ridiculously so.

Let's start with some of the good. The game is from 2004, the graphics are good, especially for the time and I think they hold up pretty well today. The game goes for a more realistic approach than something like Doom, Quake or Half-Life but it's not pretending to be Call of Duty, so it has a blend of more realistic damage but you still can find health and armor pickups.

The story is campy fun, it's basically an adventure with some sci-fi elements with a protagonist that's not quite a stereotypical action hero like in Duke Nukem or Serious Sam but you get to listen to him through the game unlike the silent protagonists of Doom and Half-Life. You have a few cut-scenes but they're short for the most part so the game moves along without long interruptions. And the game plays nice, the guns have a nice feel to it and the mechanics are good although I found myself not using all of them all the time and found that other than taking more cover and hiding more than in other classic shooters, I could play it almost the same as some other classic shooters.

Now to expand on the bad, my main complain is how hard it is. I don't have anything against hard games but this game can feel unfair and cheap in how hard it can be. You don't move as fast as in other games and you have limited stamina so you don't even have long periods of time to move fast, in the first few levels you adapt to a more cautious style using cover, deception (like distracting the AI by throwing rocks), you die a lot but you learn, adapt and change strategies and you can manage it. But when the mutated creatures start appearing the game quickly changes to unfairly hard. Some of these creatures can kill you with 1 good blow and health and armor pickups are not as abundant as they are in other games.

I don't mind being killed with one blow for sense of realism (like a blow to the head for example) so much in the first few levels, there are plenty of levels where you can shoot with a sniper from afar and the AI doesn't have perfect aim so you can take some damage if you stay moving and shooting with better aim, it doesn't feel so bad, but when you have a monster with a rocket launcher as an arm that can shoot infinite rockets at you without having to recharge (when you do have to recharge) and no apparent cool-down and a single rocket can kill you, and you shoot at it with rockets and your rockets barely make a scratch on the monster, I'm sorry, that's just not fair. In other shooters, creatures like that can be stunned and usually kill them with 1 or 2 rockets or weapons that do similar damage like grenades, but not here, and they send you to fight either a bunch of them in open areas or one or two in closed areas where you can barely dodge the rockets and barely make any damage to them when you shoot them.

If you can play this game and pass it with just your skills, more power to you, in my case, this is one of the first games that made me so frustrated it actually made me upset and I had to use cheats to decrease the damage taken by me and increase the damage done to the enemies otherwise I wouldn't have finished it.

Also, the game is outdated and apparently hasn't received the same love and attention by the modding community as others games have so you have a few mods and patches that fixes things like widescreen and other things but I still found bugs and errors, so there's that.

So if you want to go through the history of FarCry games or are an FPS fan, I do recommend playing this game, if you're better than me (which is really possible, I'm not particularly good...) you might like the challenge more than I did or if you're on a similar skill level as mine, then search for a few cheats for the particularly hard levels, mainly the last 2 are really nasty, but before that, this is a really enjoyable game that can be hard but with a good strategy can be fun and challenging.

By now, the Far Cry series from publisher Ubisoft needs no introduction; at this point, practically everyone has played Far Cry 3 at the very least. However, the first installment was exclusive to PC when it launched in 2004, but finally made its way to consoles, along with a graphic overhaul, in 2010. Despite that, not many people are aware that this first title was developed by the esteemed Crytek Studios, the masterminds behind the computer-melting game, Crysis, and the creators of the Crytek Engine.

The story is a tad aloof, but we're placed in the perspective of a man named Jack Carver; a guy who has decided to abandon his old life to run a boat-charter business in the South Pacific. Hired by Valerie Constantine, Jack secretly escorts her to an uncharted island in Micronesia. Lo and behold, after Valerie takes off, Jack's boat is blown to smithereens by a rocket and he's left floating helplessly among the isles. Though the environments are a brightly colored slice of paradise, a deep and sinister evil is lurking just below the surface; the islands are part of a genetic modification experiment gone awry, and Jack is stuck right in the middle of the abomination's takeover.

Jack's backstory is never fleshed out, and as such he comes off rather shallow. The same can be said for the rest of the characters in the game; they're all lacking depth and memorable personas. Jack himself is more or less a fusion of Duke Nukem meets Serious Sam, with his semi-witty one-liners and macho-man attitude. It's obvious that Crytek Studios weren't in the business of crafting noteworthy characters during their early years. The story is alright, although the actually storytelling could be better; it's comes off as a somewhat cryptic tale, though needlessly so. In the end, it's easy to understand what's going on, and there is a decent, though expected, plot twist.

The real meat and potatoes of Far Cry is, of course, its gameplay. It's quite a beefy first-person shooter, that's for sure; be prepared to work for each and every checkpoint and level progression, as the challenge will still pack a hard punch even on Easy difficulty. There are a total of 20 levels to be enjoyed, and though the story and objectives are linear, each map is wide open for the exploration, much like the original Crysis. The last three or four levels are absolute hell-infused torture, with all of the game's biggest and baddest monsters coming out to play in large groups. It's very reminiscent of Serious Sam, and to a lesser extent, Doom. As opposed to other entries into the Far Cry series, this title doesn't feature side quests, outposts, or any of the extras, it's all fetch, kill, and destroy linear missions.

As far as functionality and control systems are concerned, Far Cry still looks and feels great thanks to the fantastic Cry Engine. It's not a beautiful game, but it's not ugly either. The keybindings are all modern, though they can be rebound if one desires. The only complaint here is the control of any vehicles, which feature steering that is far too loose. The views can be changed from first-person to third-person while in cars, but the camera likes to act up either way, making it incredibly hard to fire at enemies. This release does still function just fine on Windows 10, without the need for patches, modifications, or extra settings. For those looking for a graphical upgrade, there is a mod for the 2010 overhaul available.

Far Cry still stands as a great classic experience that should be taken on by any FPS enthusiast. It's best described as a fusion of Serious Sam meets Doom with a light glaze of Half-Life overtop. There's a good handful of guns to play around with as well, from the P90 submachine gun, to a sniper rifle, rocket launcher, a couple of assault rifles, a shotgun, two pistols, and a machine gun. The maps and missions are decently varied in terms of landscape, though most of the gameplay takes place on top of the beautiful tropic paradise. Depending on skill level, the longevity of the campaign will last from 7-12 hours, making the standard $9.99 CAD pricetag a good deal.

Somewhere during the late 90s and early 00s, first-person shooters grew increasingly more linear and tightly-scripted. This was largely due to the development time required for a relatively small team to create more open, non-linear environments with complex 3D architecture. As much as I enjoyed some of these linear shooters (No One Lives Forever and Star Trek Voyager: Elite Force spring to mind), I was starting to miss the days where I could walk into a room and discover three or more doors leading out of it. Also a little nervous that non-linear shooters were a thing of the past.

Thankfully Far Cry allayed those fears from the get go, presenting the player with nearly endless vistas, huge islands to be explored, enemy encounters that could be approached in a variety of ways. It felt like a brand new yet also warmly nostalgic gaming experience. 

Far Cry was the first game I chose to play on a newly-built PC system back at the start of 2005. I also had Half-Life 2, Doom 3, Quake 4, Thief: The Deadly Shadows and Deus Ex: Invisible War waiting in the wings. Far Cry came free with the video card, so I decided to "get it out of the way" first, only to end up entranced for about 12-15 hours and finding it to be one of the strongest of that particular set of unplayed games.

Thank you, Far Cry, for helping bring back non-linear environments to the FPS genre at a time when it desperately needed them.

Far Cry was designed as the dream-come-true FPS game of some ambitious newcomers at the gamedev stage - Crytek studio. Their first known project turned out as the real bomb when it was released. The hype was immersive - and after all those passed years, I have to say, this game is worth its reputation. 'Thunder in Paradise' rich setout unleashes badass old-school shooter (like Doom or Half-Life) - with so many fixes as one could imagine 12 years back: outstanding visuals and physics, witty and challenging level design, clever AI behavior... And level editor for icing the cake.

I remember playing (and ending) this game in 2004-2005, with the hardest difficulty possible. The last level was utterly hard, and it changed my mentality forever. Seriously. Now I have but one fear in my life. My only fear is about ammo depletion. So far as I'm locked and loaded, let'em come!

Well, sadly, my skill was decreased since those times, so now I am good enough only at "challenging", medium-level difficulty. For the newcomers, however, I suggest starting from the basic level of difficulty - the standards were really different then. I've read many depressing comments about this game from people who decided to give it a try but were not ready for the outcome. Enemy soldiers are not aim-bots, that's I know for sure. If you're good with positioning and tactical movement in the rough terrains, if you're lucky... and if you're ready for constant reloads... Try it on!

The game is selling for such a low price, that every FPS devotee should have no problem with adding this brilliant to the collection. The only real question before buying should be - are you really bad enough for this? You can't hide behind a chest-high wall here and recover health. The enemies, once you'll allow them to spot you, will be engaging until you'll finish them all or die trying. Some of them will be crying for backup (and usually, they'll get one), some will be cornering you, while others will rush on you, using suppressive fire, grenades, and strafing moves... And all that you'll see right from the beginning!

As for downsides: saving only at checkpoints is really annoying! Sometimes those checkpoints too far one from another, sometimes, when you crouch your way around the enemy, you can not activate any checkpoint at all! And sometimes checkpoints are saving the game just the second before enemy sniper blows your head off. Some levels, otherwise quite well-performed, could become total clusterfunk due to those fixed savepoints. Like the upper level of the tanker, where you have only about 0.5 to 1 second to hide once you've climbed there before bullet hell breaks loose. Or later, in the second half of the game, where some enemies are getting on another level of the food chain... My advice here is to find a tweak guide with using a console around this problem. Or get over with it as it is!

My mark is 8/10. Clever engine and gameplay, nice physics. We don't have scarcity for FPS games, that's right. But if you need FPS where you are not tied to corridor shootouts... Where you exploring the area around before engaging - or instead of it - to learn enemy's routes, behavior, weak points... Where you have to worry about not being hit more than about fragging another dozen of dummies - now, there's still not many good games like this.

Far Cry 1 deserves it's place in the pantheon of legendary FPS games. Released in 2004, even today it is comfortably better than many so-called "AAA" games released in the modern age. At the time of coming to market, Far Cry set new benchmarks for AI, graphics and gameplay. Loading was a thing of the past, with massive maps, near-unlimited draw distance, and missions which had multiple approaches to completing. While Far Cry 1's dialogue, story, and characters are painfully cheesy and dumb, the gameplay and level design are a total blast.

You spend most of your time carefully navigating an open-world tropical island full of heavily armed and bloodthirsty mercenaries. You have a few different ways of getting around the island which includes simply going on foot, or using vehicles such as turreted jeeps, boats, and a paraglider. The game is action-packed and encourages the player to be strategic. It's really hard, even on the easiest difficulty since enemies are able to properly utilize tactical maneuvers to overwhelm and take you out, and snipers/rocketeers can spot you from far away.

Unfortunately, the vanilla version of the game on Steam has broken AI, which basically gives the enemies X-Ray vision allowing them to see you and shoot through any cover that isn't solid. I played with FCAM (Far Cry Addon Mod), which fixes the AI, enhances the graphics, adds iron sights to the weapons, introduces quicksave functionality, amongst other things. There are other ways to get around the AI issue, but they are far more tedious and less likely to work. I strongly recommend getting FCAM and playing with it enabled. Should you decide to go this route, add "-mod:FCAM" to the launch options, minus the quotation marks: this will launch the game and FCAM mod automatically, saving you from having to manually switch from the main menu.

For those complaining about the difficulty, this is not a run-and-gun shooter: the enemies are smart, and will home in on your location, and attempt to surround or flank you. Staying on the move and using cover constantly is key to success, as well as choosing your battleground carefully. 

Highly recommended to anyone who enjoys FPS games - this one cannot be missed and is a true classic.

[h1] Breaking with Old Ideas [/h1]

Far Cry, released in 2004, is an ambitious first-person shooter in the now renowned franchise owned by Ubisoft. 
In an era of corridor shooters like Doom 3 and later Half-Life 2, Far Cry differentiates itself by using a massive outdoor tropical environment instead. 
The game has a notable graphical fidelity for a game of 2004, the first instance of the “CryEngine” that would in turn become famous through the Crysis series of games. 

The story lacks substance and shows a certain disregard for narrative focus in games. Which is an aspect aforementioned games like Doom 3 and Half-Life 2 were moving away from.
But where the story is lacking in complexity, Far Cry makes up for in its gameplay and unforgiving difficulty. You die after only a few shots and so there’s a huge reliance on finding tactical paths leading to vantage points or ambushes, getting in a few critical shots on the enemy before they see you.

Sadly as much as it wants to be innovative and forward thinking, the game doesn’t always play into its strengths. A lot of segments include the very same corridors that Far Cry was trying to move away from in the genre. The game is clearly not designed to work well with these closed spaces and so it becomes tedious and unfun, it genuinely would have been a better game had they never put these corridor segments in the game to begin with. 

After a certain encounter the game's enemies change quite drastically and there’s open conflict between factions quite reminiscent of how later games tackled man vs nature in gameplay, letting both fight it out before approaching the enemy, and in instances it can be unpredictable in a tension-filled way. 

Far Cry is a game trying to move away from the design tropes that restrained its genre, but was also severely stuck in those same tropes it was trying to move away from. It remains a unique experience that showed ambition towards what could become a truly great game had it not halted itself.

Needless to say that first Far Cry is pretty old by now.
But is it good, just like you remembered it back then, or is it a piece of crap that is good only if seen through the rose-tinted glasses of nostalgia?
Welp, I'll try to answer that throughout this review.

As many people know, starting from the Far Cry 2 the series gone for full open world style,
with a main objective to accomplish and many other side activities that are optional.
In this case, we have more of a "closed open world" map design and a completely linear storyline.

[*][b]Map design.[/b]
The protagonist, Jack Carver, finds himself stranded on an archipelago, crawling with mercenaries (that kind of blew up his yacht, which is the reason he got to this place).
It is fairly open, but also fairly closed. How?
The islands have quite an amount of high, unreachable hills, mountains, etc., that show you were you are not supposed to go,
and there all the other islands, with beaten paths, beaches, tiny rivers inbetween them, that you can traverse either on foot, or via a transport.
Some places you will try to deal with enemies on your two, some places you will try to ride past (or over) blockades on the buggy,
and sometimes you will be incentivized to use water transport, like inflatable boats or a heavy-weaponised full-metal boats.
Also, there are a few hand gliders (2 or 3 for the whole game), that give you some fresh feel of complete freedom.
Until you fly into a mountain. Or a chopper. Or a party of armed angry mercs.
As a fun fact, you can shoot (even from two-handed weapons) while on a hand glider. Do not ask how. I can't answer this myself.
So, having these vehicles and some open spaces provides you some wiggle room to deal with your current objective.
Either you find a place as high as possible and shoot everyone from afar with weapon that has scope, or ride into the fight on your 4x4,
guns blazing and you being dead in half a second. Oops.

[*][b]Shooter aspect.[/b]
It is good. Guns feel pretty nicely, having the recoil, sway patterns the more you shoot them.
I must say that they aren't particularly accurate, so most of the time you'll be spraying enemies, to make sure whatever's in your iron sights won't throw a bullet back at you.
There is a satisfying amount of weapons available, so you won't get tired of the same thing over and over again.
You are mobile enough to go running-n-gunning and is fragile enough to hide behind cover from time to time.
Of course, you'll be hiding a lot more the further your progress into the game, as enemies become a walking bullet sponges.
I mean, this dude survived a 5.56 mag from a meter away because he had a kevlar. [i]Really?[/i]
This game has 4 weapons slots, that can be fit with anything you can use as a weapon.
I'd suggest [b]ALWAYS[/b] having an [b]assault rifle[/b], preferably with a scope, so you can easily wipe out enemies from close to mid-range and have ammo replenished from their guns,
and even more crucial is carrying a [b]sniper rifle[/b], since there will be a lot of times where mobs spray you with BS from, seemingly, another dimension.
This way you will at least be able to oneshot (hopefully) the bastard and continue your daily routine of mass genocide.

[*][b]Plot.[/b]
Plot is as straightforward as it gets.
You're blown out of your peaceful ride on a yacht, you get to kill the punks for doing that to you, and try to leave the islands,
with a help of a [i]mysterious[/i] dude on the other side of PDA thingy you'll find in the beginning of the game.
Then, you'll be tasked with different missions, that 80% of the time are "take the explosive there" and "use it to explode something there".
Some time after, you'll get to know that something sinister is going on around here, and you're in a middle of all it.
I won't spoil exactly what that sinister is, and yes, I know that this game is 16 years old, and yes, I know that nobody cares.
As it always is, there'll be an [i]"""unexpected twist"""[/i], that will wrap up the story, as you kill the last bad guy.

[*][b]Technical aspect.[/b]
[strike]This is the reason I started drinking.[/strike] It isn't very good.
The game worked fine for me, no crashes, no visual, sound glitches, I didn't get perma-stuck in objects, etc.
But that doesn't mean that the game isn't broken.
The bugs are mostly condensed in the first chapters, which ironically, would probably make many new players call it a steaming pile of sh*t and call it quits.
Mercs will be able to shoot you through some of the walls, a buggy will shoot you without having a gunner on a seat,
control scheme erases itself after rebooting PC (though it might be because I have multiple languages in use).
AI is broken badly, but from what I gathered, it is the Steam version that introduced the AI as it is now.
AI will vary from being braindead and not seeing you point-blank, asking whether his buddy is alright after being shot 10 times in the head before his own eyes,
to genetically modified supersoldiers, that can see you through all the flora on the level like it isn't there at all,
and being able to shoot you from a kilometer away with an AR without missing a single hit, while twitching uncontrollably like dude's on hard drugs.
Last level pretty much forces you to abuse stupidness of your enemies to pass it.

In conclusion, if you are to resist the frustration and get yourself some nostalgia, it is still a decent game.
I thank you for reading this, and wish you a great one.

[h1]Short review[/h1]

When Far Cry was released, this game finally brought out of the torpor the FPS fans have been in for too long. In an original setting of stunning beauty and despite an AI still perfectible but fierce, Far Cry is sure to seduce the fragger by its gameplay which, although basic, requires a certain caution and adds a feeling of freedom and permanent danger to make us reach a playful ecstasy. If you were looking for an excuse to finally play this game, you have it. This game is nice, and it will make you see what the first title of the now well-known franchise was about.

[h1]Long review[/h1]

Eager to forget his troubled past, Jack Carver is cushy in his boat rental office in a lost corner of the Pacific. Valerie Constantine asks him to take him to an isolated atoll. After not even a minute his brand-new boat eats a freaking rocket (god knows why) and Jack is almost drowning. He finally lands in an old Japanese bunker, dirty, stunned and dispossessed of his mysterious client. While advancing a little, our Jack, who looks furiously like the great Jean Claude Van Damme, comes across a gun and a cell phone which allows him to make contact with Doyle, his new guardian angel. And that's it, period, I'm not going to dwell on the script, because frankly, in the world of the FPS genre we can find much better but whatever. In any case, taking us to a paradisiacal atoll was, in itself, an excellent and pretty new idea at the time of the release.

After a few seconds you get out of the bunker and you are at the top of a hill with a splendid view. Nicely done landscape which contrasts by its luminosity and its colors with the monotonous tones of the bunker. "God it's beautiful" was the first words that came out of my mouth after playing it for the first time back in 2004. The fine sand, the palm trees, the rocks, the realistic water with its foam, the light that flashes, the dense vegetation when we enter the jungle, the insects that fly under your nose, everything was absolutely splendid in the simply huge exteriors of Far Cry. Yes, now the standards for "beautiful" changed but the game will not make you puke if that's what you want to know.

Yes, the map is huge for a 2004 game. And suddenly you are offered great freedom of movement. Even if in truth, this freedom is a little less great than we thought because it is often a question of taking different paths envisaged by the developers, you feel them guiding you imperceptibly with the tip of their finger, as you would push an ant. You can venture into the jungle but in the end, there will always be an impassable mountain (but never an invisible wall with walnut) which will redirect you to the final objective. But hey, I'm not going to quibble and you still have a very wide choice. These various side roads will also have another utility than allowing to replay twice differently and to feel free like Max. It can very often be useful to find a less frontal approach to an outdoor lens for example. Maybe that way you'll be less exposed to the filth that is using a heavy machine gun, unless you get yourself a good sniper post on a hill, and hey, if you swim to those crates and that you try to enter without being seen? One is always rewarded for searching the surroundings a bit instead of rushing like a monkey by the most obvious route. And even if we are a bit limited, the feeling of freedom is indeed present (more than in Deux Ex: Invisible War anyway), and that's all that matters.

I should talk about infiltration aspect of the game after many hours spent on it. Of course, you have the necessary gauges to play the tropical Sam Fisher, but playing that way seems just impossible. In fact, you can sneak around for a while, but it always ends in absolute carnage. The infiltration or rather the stealth will be useful to approach a sensitive point more easily, perfect to reach a good hideout before taking out your weapons or better, to launch a game of hide and seek and kill the guards individually. Like a Predator. The infiltration is therefore present, but it is more of a bonus than a real gameplay, Far Cry therefore remains resolutely action oriented. Basically, our primary goal is to survive in hostile environments facing numerous enemies that you don't always see. Alone in the middle of the trees, you will watch for the slightest movement, the smallest shadow, the smallest sound of footsteps and you never feel safe until you have cleared an area. And you will quickly feel the reality of the thing, especially insofar as the game does not offer quick saves but only a system of checkpoints. Of course, it's good for the atmosphere and the challenge, but you have to admit that it's also often very bad for the nerves when you have to replay a particularly difficult passage.

A problem that you will less feel during the indoor levels. We change completely here since the game becomes very linear. Often dark, these levels will bet on the feeling of oppression, paranoid at the slightest noise and claustrophobia. Strange sounds of beasts leaping over you. On more than one occasion, you will feel the fear of not reaching the next checkpoint alive and that is particularly anxiety-provoking.

Crucial point not yet addressed: the AI. In general, it fulfills its role perfectly. Outdoors, it will be able to take advantage of the size of the surroundings to take you from behind, for example, and a guard's first instinct will be to call for reinforcements or sound the alarm when he sees you. I appreciate not being spotted as if by magic and even more the fact that the aim of enemies is sufficiently imprecise to be credible but not enough to be stupid. It's a lot of fun playing hide and seek with an AI that's pretty believable in the role of the wolf. In number, the mercenaries oppose a tough resistance and therefore offer a challenge worthy of this name. However, this AI is good, sometimes pleasantly surprising, but not perfect. I regret, for example, a behavior that is sometimes a little too typical. There is also a tendency to open fire as soon as you are spotted, even if the enemy is completely exposed, a rather silly behavior. But the biggest regrets are found in the tightest interiors with mercenaries who pounce on you like morons which, in a level essentially made up of narrow corridors, is like throwing themselves on a blast of lead. In the same way, post yourself at the exit of a building giving on a courtyard, while remaining inside, and wait for the targets, you will soon have a nice pile of corpses. In fact, the more spaces the AI ​​has, the better it does and vice versa.

But despite everything, the AI ​​of Far Cry is quite decent and will give you a lot of trouble. Like the excellent single player campaign by the way. Sustained action that draws on several tables (tense gunfights and feeling of oppression) via gameplay that mixes caution and nervousness. I would say a word about physics all the same, since Crytek's engine could well compete with the very popular Havok. The funniest part is that the developers have planned various places where you can play around with the laws of gravity to send a few mercenaries to the next world. Rolling large cans or dropping containers are fun alternatives to headshoting. 

But what about multiplayer? It may be a bit of a disappointment since only one of the three game modes stands out, it is the assault mode which only has 6 maps. Too bad because if you have the patience, the multiplayer is very stimulating despite some slowness relative to the size of the cards. We are not in Counter-Strike. In any case, with such large maps and such a vast horizon, the snipers will have fun (beware of the sun which is reflected in the glasses).

To sums things up, this game is quite nice even if released in 2004. Try it out if you like Far Cry, you will not be disappointed.

This game didn’t actually age as poorly as I initially thought. Sure, the graphics don’t look so great, but the physics and the water reflection are pretty nice for its time and are kinda good even for today standards. 
The gameplay is also fun, but the game sometimes is too difficult for its own good… Don’t get me wrong, I like a challenge, but I don’t think it’s good game design having a boss fight where you gotta hit a helicopter around 6 times with explosive damage (When the game only gives you like 8 rockets) and under a limit of time (Before the ship you're standing on sinks completely) while avoiding the machinegun guy on the helicopter that can kill you in literally under a single second if you’re outta cover ON NORMAL DIFFICULTY. The game is actually full of this bullshit game design, where enemies have infinite ammo (including the rocket launcher guys) and won’t stop trying to shoot you even when you’re out of their line of sight, where enemies will easily spot and snipe you across the map (regardless of the weapon they’re using) if you’re not in prone and where enemies can see through walls and hear every movement you make, even though they’re many meters away, leaving the stealth completely useless.
It gets REALLY bad at times, but if you have enough patience you will eventually find a way to exploit the enemy AI and complete your objectives (assuming that you’re not on realistic difficulty, because this mode is literally impossible).
"But what about the easy mode", you may ask. Well, it happens that even the easy mode is challenging. It goes more like this: Easy = Normal; Normal = Hard; Anything else = The definition of insanity.
Some people say the AI in this game is very good, but I don’t really agree with that. If you get close to an enemy armed with a rocket launcher they will 100% of times shoot you anyway even though they’ll probably die in the explosion. Sometimes enemies will also kill themselves with their own grenades. I wouldn’t really call that a “good AI”, but, perhaps, they meant “for its time”?
Back to the gameplay, the gunplay itself is pretty decent, you can actually lean right and left and even prone, something you can’t do in the other main Far Cry games, but it has its flaws. One of them is how painfully slow the character runs, how quick the stamina bar runs dry and also how slowly is replenishes. The stamina bar, by the way, is also your “breath” bar, meaning that if you go underwater without any stamina your character will start drowning instantly (This is actually kinda realistic, but still annoying when it happens).
The speed you move is actually based on the weapon you’re holding, like: if you’re holding the machete, you’ll move slightly faster than when you’re holding a rifle. But if you’re holding the AW50 or the M202 (The in-game name is actually RLX-9157) your character will start moving as fast as the Internet Explorer.
The stealth still kinda exists, but as mentioned earlier, it doesn’t really “work”. If you try to melee anyone from behind, they will just hear you before you get any close from the machete’s reach. There is one (and only one) suppressed weapon in the game though, and this weapon is the MP5SD. This one actually works for killing enemies silently, but you ain’t gonna go much far with it before being spotted by everyone on the map at the same time for some bullshit reason.
Frag Grenades are not the only throwables available in the game, you can also use smoke and flash grenades, but they’re mostly useless and enemies will usually completely ignore them.
The story of the game is not very good and not very long either. Assuming that you won’t be dying all the time, of course. And I really doubt you will not die all the time, if you’re in your first playthrough and on normal difficulty.
The in-game and mainly the pre-rendered cutscenes didn't age pretty well. It’s the kind of thing you can't really watch while making a straight face.

This is worth a play through for anyone who is interested in the evolution of the Far Cry series, and the first person shooter as a genre. If you missed this at the time, or indeed weren't born at the time, going back to the archipelago may prove a little too difficult or unwieldy but there is definitely a fun game beyond the frustrations.

Before Half-Life, all a FPS needed to do was give you huge rooms and tight corridors filled with all kinds of monsters to kill, and an arsenal of preposterous weapons with which to do the killing. After Half-Life, players expected stories and action set pieces. Far Cry manages to give both, although neither are ever quite as memorable as Gordon Freeman's antics.

We play as Jack Carver, an all American bad ass who makes a buck ferrying people around a tropical paradise. One day he charters his boat to photo journalist Valerie Constantine and she brings him into a chaotic world of mercenaries, heavy artillery and an evil scientist called Krieger.

It would be another three years before Crytek would officially start melting computers with Crysis, but I imagine that this original Far Cry outing caused a few heated graphics cards back in the day. Even by our modern standards, this is a pretty game. Sure draw distances are limited, there's pop-up galore, and details are a bit lacking on the vistas, but there are still nice sky boxes and actual physical models of birds and fish inhabiting the jungle and sea.

Sound design is really strong. I played with headphones, and the jungle is just alive with noise. The ever present chirrups of crickets and the calls of tropical birds really helps sell the location. There's plenty of banter from the mercenaries when you listen in with your directional microphone, and the sounds of battle can become quite intense. The music is really good, and only gets better as the game progresses and the tension is ramped up.

Gunplay is decent throughout. Each gun has it's own characteristics and feel, but you will quickly find one or two favourites and stick with those. You are limited to only carrying four weapons at once, and by the end I had three which used the same commonly found ammunition type. This was crucial in the last few levels when you come up against enemies who are some of the spongiest bullet sponges ever to grace a game with their overwhelmingly unbalanced presence.

Combat encounters range from challenging to downright nigh on impossible. While I was never driven to rage quitting, I certainly did save scum like there was no tomorrow. I think I only played on normal, and given the deadly accuracy of enemies from half a map away, I'd hate to imagine what the more challenging settings are like. The last two or three levels will make you wince and scream and cuss like a sailor, but you should be invested enough in the story and the characters that you will force yourself to finish.

Initial Thoughts: I have just completed Far Cry, it took me just under 9 hours to finish. 

Story: This game feels straight out of a 2000s action-adventure flick; think XXX with Vin Diesel, Pierce Brosnan’s James Bond, or even the DOOM movie. It’s packed with cheesy clichés and doesn’t take itself too seriously, which actually adds to the fun and humor. It’s your classic ex-special-forces hero saves the day and gets the girl setup. Without spoiling anything, the ending is one of the most anti-climactic I’ve ever seen, almost a zero-payout after the punishment you endure in the final mission.

Characters: They’re bland and lifeless, with voice acting that borders on parody. The main character sounds like that surfer guy from the viral interview describing waves, it’s comically bad. His partner doesn’t sound anything like she looks, which only adds to the disconnect. But let’s be honest, this game wasn’t built for its story; it was built to show off the Crytek engine.

Gameplay & Mechanics: Far Cry can be downright unfair, even on the easiest difficulty. It wants you to approach missions stealthily; going into it full run-and-gun as I did will get you punished fast. Some missions and boss fights, especially the infamous final one, are absurdly difficult unless you cheese your way through them. That being said, driving sequences are fun, and weapons are satisfying to use, each with their own advantages. The MP5SD is a standout here. The rocket launcher, however, is extremely underwhelming, it’s slow and weak compared to the one enemies use (theirs absolutely wrecks you).

Graphics: Crytek is crushing it in 2004. The graphics and physics are stellar in most areas, the water effects are especially impressive, and the game still looks good by today’s standards. The only downside is the limited draw distance, which can break immersion a bit.

Final Thoughts: Far Cry stands out as a unique entry in the series; it feels more like a Crysis prototype than a traditional Far Cry sequel. It’s a not-so-serious, action-packed adventure that fits right into that early-2000s hero-movie itch.

Score: 7.0/10. As true a 7 as it gets. It does just enough right to rise above average, but the uneven balance and weak storytelling keep it from going any higher.

This is one of the OG sandbox shooters, possibly the first of its kind, and while I would love to recommend it for its historical value, the game is a frustrating experience from beginning to end. The presentation is gorgeous, and it was cool to see all of the hallmarks of the later installments appear so early, but overall the execution is very rough. This game is extremely difficult, and even on challenging I was sorely tempted to walk away. The main issue here is that the time to kill is absurdly short. Armor absorbs only a few bullets before breaking, and your healthpool is miniscule after this. Once engaged in a firefight (unless you're hiding in some bushes, perhaps the only viable strategy), enemies have a laser-focus on you, which isn't a problem per say except for the aforementioned fragility of the player character. Compounding this is that the first several levels feature many camps filled with tents, which can be shot through, and the problem becomes even clearer. The melee enemies are likewise also a pain in the ass. Cinematics are sloppy and disjointed - things happen that don't remotely seem to connect with the present action. The story is simple, which isn't unexpected, but strange quasi t&a felt out of place, like the writers and animators were not at all on the same page, and the delivery of the characters is as emotive as a brick wall.

Honestly, Far Cry is not worth your time outside of curiosity. It has a great deal of ambition, and at points the game feels very ahead of the curve, but on the whole it is neither good nor enjoyable. There's a reason most people push Far Cry 3 to newcomers.

You play as Jack Carver, an ex-Special Forces soldier (he's an ex-Navy Seals in Instincts) who works as a boat captain, chartered out near Micronesia with Valerie Constantine, a reporter who claims to want to take photographs of the Japanese bunkers nearby. She leaves you and your boat gets wrecked by some armed dudes, and soon, you wake up in a cave system where you'll have to make your way out, arm yourself, and shoot dudes to rescue Valerie once she gets herself into a sticky situation. You're aided on your travels by Doyle, a CIA agent who's masquerading as a scientist on the island to expose Dr. Krieger's experiments, the guy who's releasing Trigens, mutants, on the island. You'll be kicking the bucket many times playing this game, since enemies can have super hearing and X-Ray vision, spotting you from miles away, but mods (FCAM, for example) can fix it. Weapon choices are limited to 11 guns and you get access to 3 different grenades, and the environment, from beaches to jungles to facilities, are so beautiful. And the AI? It can suck at times (blame the Steam port), but for 2004, it was something ahead of it's time. So for 10 dollars, it's not such a bad experience for a minimum of 14 hours (I completed this in 21 hours for the full ending for obvious reasons). This game will occupy your time nicely if you give it the patience and love it needs.

So, I started playing Far Cry 1 a long time ago and I left because of how insanely hard it was. Then I wanted to give it another try and the game had erased all of my data. I didn't get that far, so no big deal. I  start a new game and I think it took me around 3-4 hours on Easy difficulty just to get to chapter 3 or 4. You see, enemies can shoot you through anything. They don't care that you're 10 miles away either; they will shoot you because why not? And this is all still happening on easy difficulty. Anyway, I left the game again for like a month, come back, and all of my save data is deleted again.

Nothing I've played compares to this game's difficulty. The broken enemy AI makes you reflect on why you were even born. The hamster on a wheel that powers the game engine can decide to delete all of your progress whenever it wants to. The Ubisoft that owns this game won't fix any of it, because they're too busy making the newest version of their busted game launcher that literally no one asked for or wanted to exist. Funnily enough, you don't need that launcher to play this game.

After having my saves deleted twice, I decided to just play it using Godmode. What makes that even funnier, is that the game gave me my saves back for no reason after I had figured out how to activate Godmode, but I didn't care anymore; the game had already defeated me at that point. There is absolutely no strategy involved when fighting enemies. You just have to die a lot and hope that you don't get spotted, sniped, or rocket spammed from 10 million miles away the next time you spawn. Imagine Mile High Club from the first Modern Warfare on Veteran, except it's stretched out for (I'm making an estimate based on my experience) about 30 hours of trial and error garbage.

So why am I still recommending this game that hurts to play?

It was funny. It was really, really funny. The cutscenes are a fever dream that break immersion constantly since they either mean nothing or they advance the story forward at light speed. The voice acting is the classiest amount of dude-bro goober. The enemies are heartless, but they are charming when they find ways to sabotage themselves for no reason. The funniest thing that happens is when your CIA friend becomes Nuclear forklift-certified in order to destroy an island full of mutated monsters because some guy on a phone told you to do that. It all comes together to form a very entertaining mess.

It also serves as an important lesson for people who want to make games. A lot of games nowadays are either very hand-holdy or incredibly difficult. When a game is too hard, it can leave someone checked out, especially when it breaks. And when a game is too hand-holdy, it can get pretty boring in a hurry since it feels like you're just wasting your time watching a game play itself. It's dangerous to chase either extreme as a developer, since it can alienate either audience if the game gets to be too difficult or too easy. Eventually, a developer might find themselves in trouble if the push for higher levels of difficulty results in a total loss of engagement with the game. It's also important for the players to play and talk about, since developers need that level of honest engagement in order to refine their development process. This game was a very negative experience, but there can be a lot of valuable lessons to learn from its failures. I'd give it a try, but I'd recommend playing on Godmode if you just want to see the whole game without losing your mind.

I feel conflicted about this game. Either i am under a Stockholm syndrome, or i genuinely liked this game. I think it is the latter.

The game has a very weak start, which takes about 4 hours (like the first 5 chapters out of 20). You get 6 fairly generic weapons, and you fight generic goons with guns. Honestly, this part of the game is just boring.

But then, the game does 2 things right. First of all, it introduces mutants, and engagements with mutants feel really different than compared to humans, almost oldschool shooters like, i would say. The game introduces about 5 different mutants in total, which are fairly distinct. The human enemies get an upgrade too, and become tougher. Also, when you kill human enemies, they drop armor. After chapter 5, they start dropping less armor points (10 instead of 30).

The 2nd thing that the game does is gives the player a lot of "power ups". It gives the player a couple of new weapons, and most importantly, they give you "cry vision", which is basically a wallhack. The new weapons are nothing new (you probably seen them hundreds of times before), but they make you much better at taking out the enemies. Honestly, you start to feel like a supersoldier by the end of the game, just like in crysis (except that in crysis you start as a supersoldier).

There are however other issues other than the "weak start". Some are related to design, and some are bugs that come only in the steam release. The bugs include bosses that don't die, and the solution being is restarting the game (not just reloading a save). By restart i mean exit and launch again, not start the game over. The other big bug is the enemies seeing you through tents. The tents are penetrable and that results in some cheap deaths. Fortunately, tents don't appear that often in the game, and mostly only appear during the first 5 chapters.

As for design issues, most people say that the game is too hard. I personally don't think like that, but i understand where they are coming from. Thing is, difficulty levels don't affect the game, because the only thing they change is the accuracy of the AI, and slightly make you do less damage. They still deal the same amount of damage though, which is why no matter the difficulty you still might strugle. Personally i completed the game on the 2nd hardest difficulty.

Also, headshots deal incredible amount of damage, just like crysis. The difference is either putting the whole magazine into the enemy, or just a couple of headshots. Also, crouching makes your shots really accurate, and reduces recoil a lot. The difference is night and day. You will have to take advantage of both of these mechanics, to progress through the game.

Far Cry remains an impressive example of an early first-person shooter built around player freedom rather than constantly forcing the action through narrow corridors. Developed by Crytek Studios and published by Ubisoft, the game follows Jack Carver, a former Special Forces operative working as a boat captain in the South Pacific. After agreeing to transport journalist Valerie Constantine to a mysterious tropical island chain, his vessel is destroyed by mercenaries. Jack survives the attack but quickly discovers that the islands conceal something far more dangerous than a private military operation.

One of the game's greatest strengths is its environment. Tropical beaches, dense forests, mountains, rivers, military camps, underground installations, and research facilities provide substantial visual and gameplay variety. Outdoor locations are often spacious enough to give players several possible approaches. Instead of simply entering an enemy base through an obvious doorway, players can scout the area from a distance, move through vegetation, attack from higher ground, use a vehicle, or begin a direct firefight. This flexibility was particularly ambitious for its era and remains one of the strongest reasons to experience the game today.

Combat rewards observation and positioning. Jack has access to pistols, assault rifles, sniper rifles, shotguns, explosives, and other weapons suited to different situations. Binoculars are especially valuable because they allow enemies to be identified before entering dangerous territory. Marking or locating hostile soldiers beforehand makes it possible to formulate an attack rather than blindly charging forward. Long-range engagements can be extremely satisfying, while close encounters are considerably more dangerous because enemies can inflict heavy damage.

Stealth provides another option, although it is less predictable than in modern games designed specifically around infiltration. Vegetation and terrain can help conceal Jack, but enemy detection sometimes feels inconsistent. Mercenaries may occasionally notice the player from surprisingly long distances or react in ways that undermine a carefully planned approach. The artificial intelligence nevertheless deserves recognition for creating opponents who can investigate disturbances, reposition themselves, pursue the player, and apply considerable pressure during firefights.

Vehicles help the islands feel larger and provide welcome changes of pace. Jeeps, boats, and other transportation allow Jack to cross substantial distances without turning exploration into a lengthy walk. Vehicles can also become part of combat encounters, particularly when approaching enemy-controlled territory. Moving between islands by boat or driving through jungle roads reinforces the campaign's adventurous atmosphere and prevents the experience from feeling like a succession of disconnected arenas.

The story gradually transforms as Jack discovers the truth behind the islands. What begins as a struggle against heavily armed mercenaries eventually introduces genetic experimentation and dangerous mutated creatures. This shift pushes the game toward science-fiction and survival-horror territory. It gives the campaign a memorable personality, although the later enemies can also make combat more frustrating. Human opponents generally provide the most enjoyable encounters because they work naturally with the game's open environments and tactical systems.

Difficulty is another aspect that modern players should consider. Far Cry can become surprisingly unforgiving, particularly during later portions of the campaign. Powerful enemies, limited opportunities to recover from mistakes, exposed environments, and occasional difficulty spikes can make certain sequences demanding. The game expects players to observe their surroundings and approach dangerous situations carefully rather than relying on constant regeneration or frequent assistance. This can be refreshing for players who appreciate challenging older shooters, but it may frustrate those accustomed to modern accessibility and checkpoint systems.

Visually, the original CryEngine technology was a major part of the game's appeal. Expansive viewing distances, tropical vegetation, reflective water, lighting effects, beaches, and enormous outdoor landscapes created an unusually convincing setting for its time. Character models, animations, textures, and some effects naturally look dated now, yet the colorful environmental design still gives the game a distinctive appearance. The contrast between beautiful tropical scenery and violent military installations also contributes strongly to its atmosphere.

Sound design complements the experience effectively. Gunfire carries enough impact to make firefights energetic, while environmental noises help sell the illusion of an isolated tropical wilderness. Enemy conversations and alerts can provide useful information when approaching hostile positions. The soundtrack is generally restrained enough to allow the environment and combat effects to establish much of the tension.

Its age is most obvious in areas such as interface design, enemy behavior, controls, checkpoint placement, and general quality-of-life features. Players coming directly from recent Far Cry installments should also understand that this is not simply an older version of the modern franchise formula. Its structure, pacing, progression, and combat philosophy belong to an earlier generation of PC shooters. There is less emphasis on collecting enormous quantities of equipment or completing a map filled with activities, and more attention is placed on surviving individual missions and navigating dangerous environments.

On Steam Deck, Far Cry is best regarded as playable with some compromises rather than a completely seamless handheld experience. The Windows version can operate through SteamOS compatibility technology, but players may need to adjust controller layouts or graphical settings and occasionally interact with interfaces originally designed for keyboard and mouse. Some text and older menus may also be less comfortable on the smaller display. Once configured properly, the single-player campaign can be enjoyed on the handheld, but users expecting a perfectly optimized console-style experience should anticipate some manual setup.

Far Cry is ultimately a significant and still entertaining shooter whose ambitious outdoor environments remain its defining achievement. Its artificial intelligence inconsistencies, demanding difficulty, aging presentation, and occasional technical roughness prevent it from feeling completely timeless, but the freedom to scout, infiltrate, snipe, drive, explore, and improvise continues to provide satisfying gameplay. For anyone interested in the origins of the series or in classic shooters that helped expand the boundaries of first-person level design, it remains well worth experiencing.
